title: Power of Two
directAnswer: A positive number is a power of two exactly when its binary form has a single 1 bit. The one-line test is `n > 0 && (n & (n - 1)) == 0`. Subtracting 1 flips the lowest set bit and turns everything below it to 1; ANDing with the original clears that lowest bit. If the result is 0, there was only one bit set. The `n > 0` guard rejects zero and negatives.

rules: `n & (n - 1)` clears the **lowest set bit**. Zero result ⇒ there was only one set bit.
Always guard with `n > 0`. For `n = 0`, `n & (n-1)` is `0 & -1 = 0`, which would falsely pass.
Negatives are never powers of two; the `n > 0` guard rejects them in one shot.
An alternative trick is `n & (-n) == n` — isolate the lowest bit and check it equals n.
Avoid looping-divide-by-2 in interviews when the bit trick exists; mention the loop, then show the O(1) trick.
whenToUse: Checking if a value is a single power of two (capacity sizing, hashing, alignment)
Validating a number has exactly one bit set
Bitmask code that requires power-of-two table sizes
antiSignals: Need the exponent k itself → use log2 / count trailing zeros, not just the boolean
Power of four specifically → extra mask to confirm the bit sits in an even position
Counting all set bits → Brian Kernighan's loop, not a single clear
Floating-point inputs → the integer bit trick doesn't apply
remember.takeaway: Powers of two are the numbers with exactly one bit set, and `n & (n - 1)` clears the lowest set bit. So `(n & (n-1)) == 0` (with `n > 0`) is the whole test — an O(1), branch-light classic.

interviewerIntent.testing: Whether you connect 'power of two' to 'one bit set' and know the n & (n-1) identity, plus whether you remember the zero/negative guard.
interviewerIntent.commonMistake: Forgetting the n > 0 guard, so n = 0 wrongly returns true, or reaching for a divide-by-two loop and missing the O(1) trick.
interviewerIntent.toStandOut: State the binary insight first, show n & (n-1), explain what subtracting 1 does to the bits, and mention the n & (-n) alternative.

problemStatement:
Given an integer `n`, return `true` if it is a power of two, otherwise return `false`.

An integer `n` is a power of two if there exists an integer `x` such that `n == 2ˣ`.
constraints: n fits in a 32-bit signed integer
x is a non-negative integer (so 1 = 2⁰ counts)
understanding: Decide whether n equals 2 raised to some non-negative power. In binary, 2ˣ is a 1 followed by x zeros — exactly one set bit. So the task reduces to: does n have precisely one bit set, and is n positive? Zero and all negatives must return false.

clarifyingQuestions.question: Does 1 count as a power of two?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: Yes — 1 = 2⁰. The bit trick handles it: 1 & 0 == 0, and 1 > 0, so it returns true.

clarifyingQuestions.question: What about 0 and negative numbers?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: Both return false. Zero has no set bits; negatives in two's complement have the sign bit set. The n > 0 guard covers both.

clarifyingQuestions.question: Is n a 32-bit or 64-bit value?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: 32-bit signed here. The trick is width-independent, but I keep the guard so the sign bit on negatives doesn't slip through.

clarifyingQuestions.question: Are loops acceptable, or do they want O(1)?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: A divide-by-two loop is O(log n) and fine as a warm-up, but the expected answer is the O(1) bit trick.

examples.explanation: 1 = 2⁰. Binary 1 has a single set bit.
Zero has no set bits and is rejected by the n > 0 guard.

diagrams.title: Picking the right approach
diagrams.caption: The loop is the warm-up; the bit trick is the O(1) answer interviewers want.

approaches.name: Divide-by-Two Loop (Warm-Up)
approaches.whenToMention: Mention as the intuitive baseline, then say 'we can do this in O(1) with bits'.
hints: A power of two keeps halving cleanly down to 1. What happens to a non-power along the way?
While n is greater than 1 and even, divide it by 2. If you ever hit an odd number above 1, it wasn't a power of two.
After the loop, n is a power of two iff it landed exactly on 1. Guard n ≤ 0 up front.
approaches.complexityReasoning: Each iteration halves n, so there are at most log₂(n) iterations. Only a couple of integer variables are used, so space is O(1).
approaches.explanation:
Repeatedly strip a factor of 2 and see whether you land on 1.

**The idea.** Every power of two divides evenly by 2 all the way down: 16 → 8 → 4 → 2 → 1. A number with any odd factor stalls — 6 → 3, and 3 is odd and bigger than 1, so 6 is not a power of two.

**The guard.** Numbers ≤ 0 can never be powers of two, so return false immediately for them; otherwise the loop on 0 or negatives misbehaves.

**The loop.** While n is even and greater than 1, divide by 2. When the loop ends, n is a power of two exactly when it equals 1.

**Why we move past this.** It is correct and only O(log n), but it loops where a single bitwise expression would do. Show it to demonstrate understanding, then present the O(1) trick.
approaches.insight: Halving is just a right shift, and 'is it still even?' is just 'is the lowest bit 0?'. That observation is the bridge from this loop to the constant-time bit trick.

dryRun.intro: Guard passes (16 > 0). Halve while even and > 1.

java.explanation: Zero and negatives are never powers of two — reject before looping.
Strip a factor of 2 while n stays even.
A clean power of two ends exactly at 1; an odd factor leaves something bigger.

python.explanation: Halve while the lowest bit is 0 (even).
Landing on 1 means n was a power of two.

pitfalls: Skipping the n ≤ 0 guard — the loop misbehaves on 0 and negatives.
Returning true whenever the loop ends, instead of checking n == 1.
Looping when an O(1) bit test is available — interviewers expect the trick.

approaches.name: Clear Lowest Set Bit — n & (n - 1) (Optimal)
approaches.whenToMention: The answer they want. Phrase it as 'a power of two has exactly one set bit, and n & (n-1) clears the lowest set bit'.
hints: Write a few powers of two in binary: 1, 10, 100, 1000. What do they all share?
Subtracting 1 from a number flips its lowest set bit to 0 and sets all bits below it to 1. What does ANDing that with the original do?
If n has a single set bit, n & (n-1) wipes it to 0. Add the n > 0 guard so 0 and negatives don't sneak through.
approaches.complexityReasoning: A single subtraction, a single bitwise AND, and one comparison — all constant-time machine operations regardless of n. No extra memory.
approaches.explanation:
Test for a single set bit by clearing the lowest one and checking nothing remains.

**The binary fact.** A power of two is `1` followed by zeros: `1`, `10`, `100`, `1000`. Exactly one bit is set. So 'is n a power of two?' becomes 'does n have exactly one set bit?' (for positive n).

**What n - 1 does to the bits.** Subtracting 1 finds the lowest set bit of n, flips it to 0, and turns every bit *below* it into 1. For `n = 1000₂`, `n - 1 = 0111₂`. For `n = 1100₂`, `n - 1 = 1011₂` — the lowest set bit (position 2) cleared, the bit below it set.

**Why the AND nails it.** `n & (n - 1)` keeps only the bits set in *both*. Since `n - 1` cleared n's lowest set bit and set everything below it (where n had zeros), the AND drops that lowest bit and preserves all higher bits of n. If n had just one bit, there are no higher bits, so the result is `0`. If n had two or more bits, a higher bit survives and the result is non-zero.

**The guard.** For `n = 0`, `n - 1` is all ones (`-1`), and `0 & -1 == 0`, which would falsely report true — so `n > 0` is required. Negatives have the sign bit set and are excluded by the same guard. That single comparison plus the AND is the whole O(1) solution.
approaches.insight: `n & (n - 1)` is the universal 'clear the lowest set bit' move — it powers Brian Kernighan's bit-count and many mask tricks. Recognizing that a power of two is the one-bit case turns the entire problem into a single application of it.

dryRun.intro: Compute n & (n-1) and check the n > 0 guard for each.

code.python:
def isPowerOfTwo(self, n: int) -> bool:
    return n > 0 and (n & (n - 1)) == 0

java.explanation: n > 0 rejects zero and negatives; (n & (n-1)) == 0 confirms exactly one set bit. Short-circuit && means the AND only runs when n is positive.

python.explanation: Guard then single-bit test; 'and' short-circuits so the bit math runs only for positive n.

edgeCases.behavior: Guard n > 0 fails → false, even though 0 & -1 = 0.
Negative; guard rejects it → false despite |16| being a power of two.
Many bits set, AND ≠ 0 → false; no overflow since no addition is done.

pitfalls: Dropping the n > 0 guard — 0 wrongly returns true because 0 & -1 == 0.
Writing (n & (n - 1)) without parentheses — & has lower precedence than ==, so it parses wrong.
Assuming it works on negatives — the sign bit makes the AND meaningless without the guard.

commonMistakes: Omitting the n > 0 guard, letting 0 pass the bit test.
Operator precedence: == binds tighter than &, so parentheses around (n & (n - 1)) are mandatory.
Reaching for a loop when the constant-time bit trick is expected.

commonMistakesDetailed.title: Missing the positive guard
commonMistakesDetailed.why: For n = 0, n - 1 is -1 (all ones), and 0 & -1 == 0, so without n > 0 the function falsely returns true for zero.

commonMistakesDetailed.title: Operator precedence trap
commonMistakesDetailed.why: In C-family languages == has higher precedence than &, so `n & (n - 1) == 0` parses as `n & ((n - 1) == 0)`, giving the wrong result.
commonMistakesDetailed.bad: return n > 0 && n & (n - 1) == 0; // parses as n & ((n-1)==0)

followupVariations.title: Power of Four
followupVariations.hint: Same single-bit test, plus check the bit sits in an even position with a 0x55555555 mask.

followupVariations.title: Number of 1 Bits
followupVariations.hint: Count set bits by repeatedly applying n &= (n - 1) — the same lowest-bit clear, looped.

followupVariations.title: Power of Three
followupVariations.hint: No clean bit trick for base 3 — use repeated division or the largest-power-of-three modulo trick.

followupVariations.title: Counting Bits
followupVariations.hint: DP where bits[i] = bits[i & (i - 1)] + 1 reuses the lowest-bit-clear identity.

patternNote: Power-of-two detection is the one-set-bit special case of n & (n - 1), the universal lowest-set-bit clear. The same identity drives Number of 1 Bits, Counting Bits, and Power of Four.
